The recurring complaints are structural rather than cosmetic: 3.3kW AC-only charging with no DC option, a 175-litre boot with the third row up, and a braked tow rating cut to 1010kg.
pros: One of only two seven-seat plug-in hybrids on sale in Australia under $90,000 — the Mitsubishi Outlander Aspire is the other, while the BYD Sealion 6, Mazda CX-60 PHEV and Ford Ranger PHEV are all five-seat — and unlike the Outlander's children-only third row this is a full-size large SUV body

Charge-sustaining economy is genuinely good for a 2.1-tonne seven-seater: CarExpert measured 6.5L/100km and Carscoops 6.4L/100km over a week without plugging in, so the car still behaves like a proper hybrid when the battery is empty rather than reverting to petrol-SUV consumption

Kia's seven-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional — it is not tied to servicing inside the Kia dealer network, unlike the conditional 10-year offers from Mitsubishi and MG — and the high-voltage battery carries its own separate seven-year/150,000km cover

For 2026 the PHEV is no longer GT-Line-only: S, Sport, Sport+ and GT-Line are all offered in AWD, each priced exactly $11,500 above the equivalent all-wheel-drive hybrid grade, so a buyer can get the plug-in drivetrain from $70,880 instead of being forced into the $86,790 flagship

Real-world electric range holds up against the claim — CarExpert saw 55km and Carscoops comfortably over 50km against the 58km WLTP figure — which covers a typical Melbourne school run and commute without starting the engine
cons: Charging is AC-only and capped at 3.3kW through a Type 2 port, with no DC fast-charging at all; Kia quotes 3 hours 26 minutes for 15-95 per cent, so a driver who cannot charge overnight at home has no practical way to keep the battery full

The 1.6L/100km label figure is meaningless in normal use: Carscoops recorded 6.4L/100km without charging against 6.0L/100km for the Sorento diesel, meaning an unplugged PHEV is slightly worse on fuel than the diesel it costs about $17,500 more than

Boot space with all three rows up drops to 175 litres because the battery sits under the second-row seat, down from 187 litres in the petrol and diesel Sorento, and the curtain airbags still do not extend to the third row

Braked towing was cut to 1010kg for the facelifted PHEV (down from 1350kg previously, and against 2000kg for the Sorento diesel), which rules out most camper trailers and is the single spec reviewers flag as a deal-breaker for towing families

Running costs are higher than the badge suggests: it requires 95 RON premium unleaded, and servicing falls due every 12 months or 10,000km at roughly $705-$765 a visit, short intervals for a family SUV

summary: The only plug-in Defender is the 110 P300e, a 221kW 2.0-litre petrol hybrid sold in two trims and no other body length. Reviewers agree it keeps everything that makes a Defender a Defender — the twin-speed transfer case, the air suspension, the 3000kg tow rating — and adds around 48km of quiet electric running that suits a Melbourne commute. Where they split is whether that is worth the money: the battery costs boot space, a third-row seat and roughly $13,000-$16,600 over the equivalent D350 diesel, and the fuel saving only materialises if the car is plugged in nightly.
pros: The only Defender you can plug in: about 48km of WLTP electric range covers a typical Melbourne commute, and it is one of the few PHEVs at any price with DC fast charging (40kW, 0-80 per cent in roughly 30 minutes) rather than AC only.

Keeps the Defender's touring hardware intact — 3000kg braked towing, a 90-litre tank, twin-speed transfer case and up to 900mm wading on air suspension — so the battery is added capability rather than a substitution.

Clears both Australian tax tests: 78g/km CO2 on the Australian label is well inside Victoria's 120g/km green-car duty threshold, and the 3.4L/100km combined figure sneaks under the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficient LCT limit that lifts the threshold from $80,809 to $91,661.

Five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty with five years of roadside assistance and six-year anti-corrosion cover, level with Volvo and BMW rather than the shorter terms Land Rover Australia used to offer.
cons: CarExpert measured 9.7L/100km on the same drivetrain once the battery was flat and never recharged — about 63 per cent above the 3.4L/100km label — so a buyer without home charging is running a 2.6-tonne car on a small four-cylinder engine and paying for it in fuel.
The pack eats the boot: Land Rover quotes up to 116 litres less loadspace than a non-hybrid 110 and a loadspace floor raised 36mm, leaving 853 litres behind the second row.
No third row. Land Rover does not offer the seven-seat Family Pack on the P300e, so a family that needs six or seven seats has to take a D350 110 or step up to a 130.
Braked towing falls to 3000kg against 3500kg for the D350 and P425, and the PHEV carries roughly 100kg more kerb weight, so it is the worst Defender in the range for a heavy trailer.

At $131,100 and $143,200 before on-road costs it asks $13,000-$16,600 more than the D350 X-Dynamic SE and HSE, and it is well past the $75,000 cap in the 2027 FBT phase-down as well as both LCT thresholds.

summary: The C10 is Stellantis-distributed Leapmotor's mid-size electric SUV, sold in Australia as a deliberate value play against the Tesla Model Y and Kia EV5 with list prices from the mid-$40,000s. Australian reviewers broadly agree on the package — RACV, CarExpert and CarsGuide all praise its limousine-like rear legroom, Maserati-tuned ride comfort and equipment level, and CarsGuide's 2026 BEV Design review scored it 7.5/10 after an over-the-air update tamed the intrusive driver-assist alerts. Where they diverge is how much the usability faults matter: the missing Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, everything-in-the-touchscreen layout and fiddly key card drew consistent criticism, and Chasing Cars marked the related C10 down to 5.5/10 for grabby brakes and numb steering, while RACV explicitly warned buyers about brand risk given Leapmotor's tiny local volume.
pros: Roughly $10,000 under a Tesla Model Y and several thousand under a Kia EV5 Air, with a panoramic roof, 14.6-inch screen and 17 driver-assist systems standard even on the $45,888 Style
Class-leading rear legroom on a flat floor — reviewers consistently rate the second row as the C10's standout, ahead of the Model Y and EV5 — plus a 581L boot expanding to 1410L
Ride comfort was tuned with Maserati chassis input and RACV found it smothers poor surfaces rather than fidgeting like most cheap EVs on 20-inch wheels
The $49,888 Design LR gets an 81.9kWh battery, 800V architecture and 180kW DC charging (30-80% in about 22 minutes) for the same price the smaller-battery Design used to cost
Cheap to keep: five services capped at $2000 total ($400 each, 12 months/20,000km) and a five-star ANCAP rating from 2024 testing
cons: No Apple CarPlay or Android Auto on any grade, with mirrors, vents and most functions buried in the touchscreen and no physical console buttons
The entry Style is stuck on the old 69.9kWh pack and 84kW DC charging — roughly half the Design LR's peak rate — so the $4000 step up buys a materially different car, not just trim
Leapmotor cut the C10's warranty from seven years/160,000km to six years/150,000km for MY25, so it now trails the seven years offered by Kia, MG, Deepal and Geely

Weak resale outlook: Leapmotor delivered only 579 C10s in Australia in 2025 and 39 in the first two months of 2026, and dealers are already listing stock in the high-$30,000s against a $45,888 list price
Numb steering, grabby friction brakes that are hard to modulate in traffic, no frunk, and a key-card entry system reviewers called convoluted enough that Leapmotor has admitted a rethink

summary: The NX 450h+ is the only plug-in hybrid in the Lexus NX range — the far more common NX 350h is a conventional hybrid with no plug — and it pairs an 18.1kWh battery with a 2.5-litre petrol four for 227kW and all-wheel drive. Its distinguishing trait is that it stays frugal once the battery is flat: Australian testers record about 5.4-6.0L/100km in charge-sustaining running, where most European PHEVs of this size drink 8L/100km or more. Reviewers rate the refinement, build and the newly added $84,500 Luxury grade, but are consistently critical of the $96,000 F Sport's value against cheaper plug-in rivals, the 6.6kW AC-only charging with no DC option, and an official 87km range claim that is NEDC-derived and about 15 per cent above the European WLTP figure.
pros: Charge-sustaining economy is genuinely low for a 2.05-tonne premium SUV: Chasing Cars measured about 6.0L/100km running on petrol alone with the battery depleted over a ~1000km long-term test, and CarExpert saw 5.7L/100km across a mostly-highway week — so an owner who cannot plug in still gets Toyota hybrid consumption rather than the 8-9L/100km typical of European PHEVs

Adding the NX450h+ Luxury AWD at $84,500 in late 2025 cut $11,500 off the price of entry to the plug-in drivetrain, which previously required the $96,000 F Sport, and it keeps the same 18.1kWh battery, 227kW output and e-Four all-wheel drive as the flagship

Lexus Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, and the hybrid battery carries separate 10-year unlimited-kilometre cover that can be extended a further 10 years through annual health checks at a Lexus dealer

Boot space is not sacrificed to the plug-in hardware — the battery sits under the cabin floor, so the 450h+ keeps the same 520-litre boot as the NX 350h hybrid, unlike the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-60 PHEV which both lose volume to their packs

Real-world electric range is usable rather than token: Australian testers report 53-70km on a full charge, enough for a typical Melbourne commute, and the car will hold EV mode to 135km/h rather than firing the engine at highway speeds
cons: Charging is AC-only at a maximum 6.6kW with no DC fast-charge capability at all, and the supplied cable is a 10A domestic lead that CarsGuide timed at roughly six hours for 35-100 per cent — a buyer without a home wallbox has no practical way to keep the battery full, at which point the car is simply an expensive NX 350h

The advertised 87km electric range is an NEDC figure mandated by ADR 81/02 for the Australian energy label; the equivalent European WLTP figure is 70-74km, so the headline number overstates the range by roughly 15 per cent before real-world driving is considered

The 1.3L/100km label consumption is meaningless in normal use — EV Central measured 5.4L/100km and CarExpert 5.7L/100km — and the car requires 95 RON premium unleaded, so the fuel bill is roughly four times what the sticker implies

At $96,000 before on-roads the F Sport sits above the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold and draws direct comparison with the Audi Q5 and BMW X3; EV Central scored it 3/5 on the basis that it is 'just not that rare or special any more' against Chinese plug-in hybrids costing $40,000-$60,000 less

Braked towing is capped at 1000kg, well under the 2000kg-plus of comparably sized diesel and petrol SUVs, and the NX still carries its 2022 ANCAP rating without the centre front airbag newer rivals fit

summary: The RX 450h+ is the only plug-in grade in the Lexus RX range — the RX350h and the flagship RX500h are conventional hybrids with no plug at all — and it pairs an 18.1kWh battery with a 2.5-litre petrol four for 227kW and all-wheel drive. Australian reviewers rate it highly for refinement, the 612-litre boot and a charge-sustaining thirst of roughly 6.5-7.0L/100km once the battery is flat, which is well under what similarly sized European plug-ins drink. The recurring criticisms are the modest 67km WLTP electric range against a BMW X5 xDrive50e's 101km, AC-only 7kW charging with no DC capability, a 1500kg tow rating, and the fact that the $123,650 Sports Luxury asks flagship money for a car whose $105,350 Luxury twin shares the whole drivetrain.
pros: The $105,350 RX450h+ Luxury added in November 2025 undercuts the Sports Luxury by $18,300 while keeping the identical 18.1kWh battery, 227kW output and e-Four all-wheel drive — it drops 21-inch wheels, adaptive suspension, adaptive headlights, the hands-free tailgate and the premium audio, but nothing that affects range or running cost

Charge-sustaining consumption is genuinely low for a 2.1-tonne large SUV: EV Central measured roughly 6.5-7.0L/100km with the battery depleted and the US EPA rates it at 35mpg (6.7L/100km) in hybrid mode, so an owner who cannot plug in still gets Toyota hybrid economy rather than the 9L/100km-plus typical of a large European PHEV

The 612-litre boot (1678 litres seats-down) is unchanged from the petrol and hybrid RX because the battery sits under the cabin floor — the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-60 PHEV both surrender load space to their packs
Lexus Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the hybrid battery is covered separately for 10 years, and servicing is capped at $695 per visit for five years or 75,000km

Unlike PHEVs that simply revert to the petrol engine when the battery empties, the RX drops into full Toyota-style hybrid operation and recharges the pack on the move, and it will hold EV mode to 135km/h rather than firing the engine at highway speed
cons: The 85km electric range Lexus Australia advertises is an NEDC figure carried by the ADR 81/02 energy label; the European WLTP figure for the same car is 67-69km, so the headline overstates the range by around 25 per cent before real-world driving is considered, and Australian testers recorded 55-60km

Charging is AC-only at 7kW with no DC fast-charge option, so a full recharge takes just under three hours on a wallbox and most of a working day on a household socket — a buyer without home charging is paying a large premium over an RX350h for a battery they cannot keep full

The 1.3L/100km label consumption is meaningless in use: it assumes every trip starts fully charged, where real Australian tests land at 4.8-5.1L/100km with regular plugging in and 6.5-7.0L/100km without, roughly five times the sticker

Braked towing is capped at 1500kg, below the 2000kg the same car is rated for in Europe and well under the 2400-2500kg of the Volvo XC90 T8 and Mercedes GLC/GLE plug-ins, and there is no spare wheel — only a repair kit

At $123,650 the Sports Luxury sits $32,000 above the fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold of $91,661 and buys a five-seat SUV with less electric range than a BMW X5 xDrive50e; CarsGuide called the EV-only range 'relatively short' for the money and the Luxury grade is the value pick by a wide margin

summary: Mazda's P50e plug-in hybrid pairs a 2.5-litre turbo petrol engine with a 17.8kWh battery for a claimed 76km of EV-only range and brisk 5.8-second 0-100km/h performance, wrapped in Mazda's most upmarket cabin. Reviewers rate the interior materials and safety kit highly and note the boot doesn't shrink for the battery pack, but they consistently flag drivetrain roughness — jerky low-speed transmission behaviour, occasional 'tug-of-war' shunt between engine and motor, and creaks reviewers say feel unresolved for the price. With the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids gone since April 2025, reviewers are also blunt that the economics only work for buyers who charge at home every night; leave it unplugged and fuel use climbs sharply.
pros: 76km claimed WLTP electric range (55-60km real-world per CarExpert) covers most Australian commutes on electricity alone, backed by a 241kW/500Nm combined output good for 5.8-5.9 second 0-100km/h
477L boot with seats up and 1726L seats-down is identical to the petrol and diesel CX-60 — unlike many PHEV rivals, the battery pack doesn't cost you cargo space
2500kg braked towing capacity matches the petrol/diesel CX-60 and beats most mid-size PHEV SUV rivals, plus a 1500W vehicle-to-load outlet in the boot
5-star ANCAP (2022, tested to Euro NCAP protocols) across the range, and the high-voltage battery carries an 8-year warranty on top of the 5-year vehicle term
Combined-cycle 49g/km CO2 and 2.1L/100km comfortably qualify every grade for Victoria's green passenger-car duty rate and the higher fuel-efficient LCT threshold
cons: Reviewers describe unresolved drivetrain manners: 'bunny hops' at low speed, a 'tug-o-war' sensation between engine and electric motor, and creaks CarExpert called 'not confidence inspiring' for a flagship-priced Mazda

Once the battery is depleted it's a ~2.2-tonne turbo-petrol AWD SUV — CarsGuide's real-world test (two charging stops over 600km) implies combustion-only running closer to 8-9L/100km versus the 2.1L/100km label, and reviewers note fuel use 'climbs a lot' if you can't charge at home

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease case that drives this site now hinges entirely on the fuel-efficient LCT and green duty concessions, not a tax-free benefit — several reviewers flag this as undermining the CX-60 PHEV's original value pitch
Azami Sp and Azami Takumi list at $83,990 and CarsGuide/CarExpert both flag CX-60 servicing costs as 'on the higher side' versus mainstream SUV rivals
200kg heavier than the equivalent G40e petrol CX-60 according to Mazda's own guide, which reviewers link to the firmer, occasionally unsettled ride reported even in Touring-spec cars

summary: The CX-80 P50e is the stretched three-row version of the CX-60 plug-in hybrid, using the same 2.5-litre petrol four, 17.8kWh battery and 241kW/500Nm combined output in a body long enough for seven seats. Reviewers rate it the best-riding and quickest CX-80 and praise the cabin quality and genuinely usable third row, but they are consistent that the electric range is modest for the money, the boot behind row three is small, and that a July 2026 price cut of $7,650-$8,119 reset the whole range downward. Opinion splits on ride: Chasing Cars calls the PHEV the best of the CX-80 line-up while other testers still find the secondary ride firm and the steering heavy around town.
pros: Now $68,100-$85,300 list after Mazda cut CX-80 PHEV prices by $7,650-$8,119 on 23 July 2026, putting the P50e just $5,000 above the equivalent G40e petrol or D50e diesel six

Every grade posts 2.7L/100km and 64g/km on the combined cycle, so all four clear both the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficient LCT test and Victoria's 120g/km green-duty ceiling — the $85,300 Azami SP pays no LCT as a result
The battery sits under the floor, so the 258L/566L/1971L boot figures are the same as the petrol and diesel CX-80 — no cargo penalty for the plug, and braked towing stays at 2500kg
241kW/500Nm makes it the quickest CX-80; Chasing Cars rates the PHEV's primary ride the best in the range, and 5-star ANCAP (2024, 92% adult occupant) covers all powertrains
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the high-voltage battery is covered for eight years, and capped-price servicing runs about $620-$700 a year over seven years
cons: 65km ADR (61km WLTP EAER) electric range is short for a $68k-plus PHEV — The Beep expects 55-60km in the real world and says nightly charging is 'essentially mandatory' to justify the $5,000 premium over the diesel

With the battery flat it is a 2237kg seven-seater on a 2.5-litre atmo four: Driving Enthusiast measured 7.0L/100km and Chasing Cars 'mid-to-high sixes', roughly two and a half times the 2.7L/100km label, so the case collapses for anyone without home charging
Only 258L behind the third row, well short of a Kia Sorento or Hyundai Santa Fe, and there is no spare wheel — just a repair kit
AC charging only at 7.2kW with no DC capability, so a depleted battery needs about 2.5 hours on a wallbox and cannot be topped up usefully on a road trip

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and the GT at $75,100 sits $100 above the $75,000 cap that will matter for FBT purposes from 2027 — the Touring at $68,100 is the only grade with clear air beneath it

summary: The EQA is Mercedes-Benz's entry-level electric SUV, essentially a battery-electric GLA with a front-mounted motor and the brand's usual small-SUV proportions. Australian reviewers consistently praise its refined, adaptive-damper ride and slick MBUX cabin, but mark it down for a WLTP range and boot space that trail cheaper, more spacious rivals now on sale locally. It reads as a car for buyers who want three-pointed-star badge appeal and a comfortable, quiet cabin rather than the last word in efficiency or outright value.
pros: Refined, well-damped ride quality even on larger wheels, reviewers say it feels bigger than its footprint
Smooth, linear power delivery from the single front motor makes it easy and relaxing to drive in town
Upscale MBUX cabin with twin 10.25-inch displays and quality materials typical of the brand
Now priced under the luxury car tax threshold across the range, helped by repeated local price cuts
cons: Reviewers note numerous rivals offer better range and/or value for similar or less money
Compromised rear legroom and a smaller-than-expected boot due to battery packaging
Divisive EQ-era styling elements, some reviewers say the design is starting to look dated
WLTP range and real-world efficiency trail newer competitors despite the premium price

summary: The EQB is a battery-electric version of Mercedes-Benz's boxy GLB small SUV, and its point of difference in Australia is a standard third row in a car under 4.7 metres long. Reviewers are consistent that it rides and insulates like a Mercedes and that the packaging is clever, but equally consistent that the third row is a 5+2 for children, that 100kW DC charging and roughly 350km of real-world range are behind the class in 2026, and that the money buys less car than the badge suggests. It is now a run-out model, with the GLB Electric replacing it locally in the final quarter of 2026.
pros: One of the very few seven-seat EVs on sale here under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT cap, and the third row is standard on all three variants rather than the $2,900 option it once was
Rides pliantly and quietly even on the standard 20-inch wheels, with sound insulation Australian reviewers rate as a clear step above mainstream electric SUVs
Second row slides through 140mm of travel, so third-row legroom can be traded against boot space rather than being fixed
Compact 4,684mm length and 210mm ground clearance make it far easier to park and garage than a Kia EV9, which needs a $97,000 entry price for the same seat count
Advertised price includes a three-year service plan package and 12 months of Chargefox public charging, which offsets Mercedes-Benz's high standalone servicing costs
cons: Only 130 litres of boot space with all seven seats in use, which CarExpert put behind a Volkswagen Tiguan Allspace in every seating configuration
The third row is explicitly a 5+2: Mercedes-Benz specifies occupants under 1.65m tall, and headroom runs out for adults
DC charging peaks at just 100kW, around half what a Kia EV9 or Tesla Model Y will take, so long-trip stops are noticeably longer
CarExpert measured 19.1kWh/100km in mixed driving against the 536km WLTP claim, cutting realistic range to roughly 350km

Out of production since January 2026 and superseded locally by the GLB Electric in Q4 2026, which leaves resale exposed; at $90,000 the 250+ also has only $1,661 of headroom under the FBT-exemption cap, so one option pack can cost a novated-lease buyer the exemption

summary: The GLC 350e 4MATIC is Mercedes-Benz Australia's first non-AMG plug-in hybrid GLC, and its 25.28kWh usable battery is roughly a third larger than most rivals' — 107km of WLTP electric range is enough that many owners will use the petrol engine only on country trips. Australian reviewers are consistently positive about the calibration and the near-silent EV mode, and note that at $99,900 it undercuts both the GLC 300 petrol it outperforms and the BMW X3 30e. The recurring criticisms are the 2.3-tonne kerb weight, a boot that loses its underfloor storage and spare wheel to the battery, and a five-year service plan that Chasing Cars priced at $7350.
pros: 107km of WLTP electric range from a 25.28kWh usable battery is the longest of any plug-in hybrid SUV under $110,000 in Australia — roughly double the Lexus NX 450h+ (87km) and Volvo XC60 T8, and enough that a typical Melbourne commute never starts the engine

Charges properly for a PHEV: 11kW AC three-phase gets 0-100 per cent in about 2h45m, and it is one of very few plug-in hybrids on sale here with DC fast charging (up to 60kW, 10-80 per cent in about 29 minutes), so a driver without a home charger still has an option

At $99,900 before on-road costs it lists $5200 below the GLC 300 4MATIC petrol it comfortably out-accelerates — 230kW/550Nm combined, 0-100km/h in 6.7 seconds — which is unusual for a plug-in hybrid, and it is 10kW/100Nm up on the $104,800 BMW X3 30e
Braked towing is rated at 2400kg, well ahead of the Kia Sorento PHEV's 1010kg and the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 1600kg, so the battery has not cost it usefulness as a tow car
Mercedes-Benz Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and is not tied to servicing inside the dealer network
cons: The 1.2L/100km combined label is meaningless once the battery is flat: Australian testers recorded 7.3L/100km (Chasing Cars), 7.8L/100km (NRMA, CarsGuide) and 8.8L/100km (CarExpert) in charge-sustaining mode on 95 RON premium, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is running a 2.3-tonne petrol SUV and the whole case for the car collapses

The battery sits over the rear axle and takes the boot from the GLC 300's 620 litres to 590, removes the underfloor storage entirely and replaces the spare wheel with a repair kit — the floor is no longer flat

Servicing is expensive even by German standards: Chasing Cars quotes $7350 for a five-year plan on 12-month/25,000km intervals, roughly ten times what a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV costs to service over the same period

It sits well above both Luxury Car Tax thresholds at $99,900 and above the $75,000 FBT cap, and since the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids ended on 1 April 2025 there is no novated-lease advantage left to offset that

Kerb weight is about 2316kg — some 200kg more than the GLC 300 — and reviewers note the extra mass in direction changes and under brakes, though the air-free steel-spring suspension copes better than expected

summary: The MG4 is consistently rated by Australian reviewers as one of the best-value small EVs on sale, combining sharp pricing with genuinely engaging rear-wheel-drive handling that punches above its budget-hatch positioning. The 2026 update fixed earlier interior gripes (better seats, more responsive touchscreen) and added the entry-level Urban variant, which reviewers praise for segment-busting cabin space and a surprisingly mature ride for the money. Common criticisms are a fiddly climate interface, an overactive speed-limit warning chime, and a boot that's merely adequate rather than class-leading.
pros: Sharp pricing relative to range and equipment, undercutting most EV rivals
Engaging, well-sorted rear-wheel-drive handling and steering feel
Spacious, upmarket-feeling cabin for the price, especially in Urban trim
Strong standard safety suite (adaptive cruise, AEB, blind spot monitoring)
Quick DC charging (10-80% in around 25-30 minutes)
cons: Boot space is only middling for a hatch (350-382L)
Few physical controls; climate functions buried in the touchscreen
Overactive speed-limit and driver-attention warning chimes annoy some reviewers
XPower's real-world range drops noticeably under highway/AWD use

summary: The HS Super Hybrid is MG's plug-in version of its mid-size SUV, and its 120km WLTP electric range is the longest of any PHEV SUV under $55,000 in Australia — enough that most buyers with a driveway charger will rarely burn petrol. Reviewers agree the powertrain is the drawcard and that the car is comfortable and well equipped, but are consistently unimpressed by the chassis: 220kW through the front wheels overwhelms the standard tyres, and the steering is remote. The catch is charging, since the car takes AC only and cannot DC fast-charge at all, so the whole value case collapses for anyone who has to rely on public infrastructure.
pros: 120km of WLTP electric range from a 24.7kWh (23.2kWh usable) LFP pack beats the GWM Haval H6 PHEV's 106km, the BYD Sealion 6 Essential's 92km and the Jaecoo J7 SHS's 90km, and carsales and EV Central both verified 100km-plus of real-world EV running before the engine woke up.

MG advertises a 10-year/250,000km warranty, but that term is conditional on servicing exclusively within the MG dealer network; the unconditional cover a buyer gets regardless is seven years/unlimited kilometres, and the drive battery is covered on the same terms as the vehicle.
The 24.7kWh pack costs nothing in packaging: 507 litres seats-up and 1484 litres folded are identical to the petrol and Hybrid+ HS, where most PHEVs give up boot floor to the battery.

220kW/350Nm combined and a 6.8-second 0-100km/h make it the quickest thing in the price bracket, and carsales covered 809km on 49.95 litres plus one charge, supporting MG's 1000km-plus combined-range claim.
cons: There is no DC fast-charging capability at all — AC only, at up to 6.6kW — and carsales measured 16 hours 16 minutes for a full recharge on test, so this is a car that only makes financial sense if you can leave it plugged in at home overnight.

Once the battery is flat it is just a heavy petrol SUV: the NRMA recorded about 6.0L/100km over 230km of suburban running in hybrid mode and carsales saw 5.9L/100km on a long highway leg, against MG's 'under 5.0L/100km' claim and a 0.7L/100km combined label figure that is meaningless as a running cost.

Reviewers at carsales and the NRMA both single out traction: the standard tyres cannot put 220kW through the front axle in the wet, and the steering is described as disconnected — the Sealion 6 Premium AWD and Haval H6 PHEV AWD have driven axles at both ends for similar money.

Advertised pricing swings hard — MG cut $5,000 off the range for an EOFY campaign in June 2026, taking the Excite to $42,990 drive-away — which is good for a buyer timing a deal but poor for resale, and PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025 so there is no novated-lease tax shelter to offset it.

summary: The MG S5 EV is the ZS EV's rear-drive replacement and is widely described by Australian reviewers as MG's most convincing model to date: a conventional, well-resolved small-to-mid electric SUV with a 453-litre boot, five-star ANCAP and pricing that sits under the Kia EV3. Reviewers agree the 62kWh car is the one to buy — the 49kWh Essence's 335km WLTP range draws consistent criticism as thin for the money — and the MY26 update added 25kW and 25km of range to the 62 at an unchanged $47,990. Opinion splits on the chassis: CarExpert and Chasing Cars rate the body control and steering response highly, while CarsGuide finds the steering too light and the styling derivative, and several testers note a ride that turns brittle over sharp-edged bumps.
pros: Up to 10 years/250,000km warranty (7 years/unlimited km if serviced outside the MG dealer network) — matching the 7-year cover from Kia, Chery and Geely and beating BYD's 6, with more on offer if you stay with MG servicing
MY26 Essence 62 gained 150kW/350Nm (up from 125kW/250Nm), cutting 0-100km/h from 8.6 to 7.0 seconds and lifting WLTP range 425 to 450km, at the same $47,990 list price
453L boot with underfloor storage, expanding to 1441L seats-down, plus a flat rear floor and genuine three-across rear seating — well ahead of the MG4 hatch's 350-382L and level with the Kia EV3
Five-star ANCAP (2025) with 90% adult occupant protection, and an MG Pilot Custom shortcut that lets you switch off individual driver-assist chimes without menu-diving
150kW DC charging gives a 30-80% top-up in about 19 minutes, and the LFP chemistry tolerates routine 100% charging
cons: Essence 49's 335km WLTP range is the range's weak point — CarExpert's verdict is that the '62 battery is far better than 49', and the $5000 step up buys 115km
The 10-year warranty is conditional on every scheduled service being done inside the MG dealer network; miss one and cover reverts to 7 years
Suspension can be harsh over sharp-edged urban bumps, and CarsGuide criticises steering that is 'too light and lacks communication'
No child presence detection, which cost it points in ANCAP's child occupant and safety assist categories (79% safety assist)

Weak Australian resale for the brand — used MG4s are retaining around 50% at three years against a ~60% EV market average, and MG's recurring drive-away and $1000-off campaigns keep resetting the market price

summary: Mini's third-generation electric Cooper hatch is, by broad Australian reviewer consensus, the most entertaining EV in its price bracket — CarsGuide scored the driving experience a perfect 10 and Chasing Cars called it one of the most enjoyable electric cars on sale here — but the same reviewers keep landing on the same objection: it is a very small, very expensive car. Mini Australia deleted the cheaper Cooper E in 2025, so the range now opens at $58,990 before on-road costs for the 400km Cooper SE, roughly $20,000 above an equivalently sized MG 4. Opinion splits hardest on the ride: some testers treat the taut, fidgety damping as part of the go-kart appeal, others find it wearing on suburban roads, and the JCW E does without the adaptive dampers the petrol JCW gets.
pros: Genuinely engaging chassis — sharp steering and go-kart agility that no other electric hatch near the price matches, per CarsGuide (10/10 driving) and Chasing Cars
Quick for a small hatch: 160kW/330Nm and 0-100km/h in 6.7s in the Cooper SE, 190kW and 5.9s in the JCW E
The 9.4-inch circular OLED touchscreen is a real design statement rather than a generic tablet, and reviewers rate the interface fast and genuinely fun to use
Every variant sits well under the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so a novated-lease buyer keeps the exemption even on the top JCW E at $63,990
High-voltage battery covered for 8 years on top of the 5-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty
cons: 210-litre boot is among the smallest of any EV on sale in Australia — under half the 470 litres of a Skoda Elroq, and only 800 litres with the rear seats folded
Strictly a four-seater with token rear legroom; CarExpert's 185cm tester could not sit behind his own driving position, and CarsGuide called the rear backrests too upright for adults
Real-world consumption of 17-18kWh/100km against the 14.7kWh/100km claim drops usable range to roughly 300km from the 49.2kWh battery
Expensive for the metal: an MG 4 Essence 64 is $37,510 and a Tesla Model 3 RWD $54,900, both far more practical, and Mini offers only one interior trim on the SE
95kW peak DC charging is modest — 30 minutes for 10-80 per cent, where similarly priced rivals manage well over 100kW

summary: The March 2026 update gave Australia's longest-serving plug-in hybrid a 22.7kWh battery, 221kW and a locally developed suspension and steering tune, and reviewers agree the ride and steering are genuinely better than the pre-update car even if 20-inch wheels still let sharp bumps through. Where they split is value: the extra 86km of WLTP electric range and the unique seven-seat Aspire earn praise, but prices rose $1700-$3000 and the range now sits well above cheaper Chinese plug-in rivals that offer more EV range for less. The charging hardware is the consistent complaint, with a CHAdeMO DC port on a standard that is disappearing from Australian chargers and only 3.6kW AC charging.
pros: 86km of WLTP electric range from the new 22.7kWh pack, up from 20kWh and 84km NEDC on the pre-update car; CarsGuide saw about 80km in real-world urban running, enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute without starting the engine
The Aspire is the only seven-seat plug-in hybrid at this price - the BYD Sealion 6, Mazda CX-60 PHEV and Toyota RAV4 PHEV are all five-seat only
1600kg braked towing across the whole PHEV range, roughly double the BYD Sealion 6 Essential's 750kg and enough for a small camper or box trailer

Mitsubishi advertises a 10-year/200,000km warranty and 10 years of capped-price servicing (about $550 a year), but that term is conditional on every scheduled service being done inside the Mitsubishi dealer network; walk away from the dealer and the cover reverts to 5 years/100,000km. The drive battery is separately warranted for 8 years/160,000km

Springs, dampers and steering were re-tuned in South Australia for the 2026 update, and Australian reviewers report noticeably less float and better-weighted steering at speed than the car it replaces
cons: DC fast charging uses a CHAdeMO plug, a standard being decommissioned across Australian public charging networks, and AC charging is capped at 3.6kW so a full recharge takes about 6.5 hours on a home wallbox

The 1.2L/100km NEDC label figure only holds if you start every trip fully charged - Mitsubishi's own battery-depleted figure is 6.7L/100km, and CarsGuide measured around 10L/100km when the engine is actively charging the pack, so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging

The 2026 update added $1700-$3000 across the range, putting the ES at $58,990 and the Exceed Tourer at $74,490; reviewers call the flagship overpriced next to cheaper plug-in rivals with more electric range

The Aspire's third row leaves only 191 litres of boot behind it and is not covered by the curtain airbags, which extend to the first two rows only - it is a children-only occasional space, not a genuine seven-seater
The 2.4-litre engine is audibly coarse when it cuts in, described by reviewers as sounding like a vacuum cleaner from inside the cabin

summary: Nissan's only EV in Australia is a quiet, comfort-tuned mid-size SUV that finally went on sale here in September 2025, roughly six years after its global reveal, and Australian reviewers consistently rate it competent rather than class-leading. Its strongest cards are the 10-year/300,000km conditional warranty, better-than-claimed real-world efficiency and a 1500kg tow rating on the dual-motor Evolve; against that, 130kW DC charging and a fidgety ride over sharp bumps leave it behind newer rivals. Verdicts diverge on value: testers praise the drivetrain refinement and cabin isolation, but most call the list pricing optimistic next to a Tesla Model Y, BYD Sealion 7 or Kia EV5.
pros: 10-year/300,000km warranty if every service is done at a Nissan dealer, with $299 capped-price servicing; stay outside the dealer network and it reverts to 5 years/unlimited km, short of Kia's unconditional 7
Real-world efficiency beats the WLTP claim: Australian testers recorded mid-17kWh/100km around town and 557km from the 87kWh Advance+ against its 504km WLTP figure
Evolve e-4ORCE is rated to tow 1500kg braked — five times the Kia EV5 Air's 300kg — and does 0-100km/h in 5.6s from 290kW/600Nm
Unusually quiet cabin and comfort-biased seating, backed by a 5-star ANCAP rating and a nationwide Nissan dealer network rather than an online-only channel
cons: DC charging peaks at only 130kW, so 10-80% takes 35-40 minutes — roughly double an 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 or Kia EV6
Engage and Advance are stuck with 385km WLTP from the 63kWh pack; the 87kWh battery costs $63,840 in Advance+ form, an $8,000 step up from the base car
Suspension reacts abruptly to sharp bumps and the Evolve's 20-inch wheels make the ride busy on coarse Melbourne surfaces
No front boot on any variant, a high rear floor that leaves rear passengers knees-up with negligible toe room, and wired-only Android Auto
Resale risk is real: 127 deliveries in 2025 and ~104 in the first four months of 2026, with factory bonuses near $7,000 and $49,990-$53,990 driveaway offers appearing within a year of launch

summary: The Polestar 4 is a coupe-styled mid-size electric SUV that Australian reviewers rate highly for its involving, well-composed driving manners, spacious and upmarket cabin, and genuinely competitive pricing against premium rivals like the Porsche Macan Electric. Its standout talking point is the deletion of a conventional rear window in favour of a camera-fed digital mirror, a decision reviewers describe as a workable, even class-leading, trade for headroom but not a universally comfortable one. Value is undercut by a lengthy, pricey options list and a control layout that pushes nearly everything through the touchscreen.
pros: Involving, well-controlled ride and handling that belies the car's size, with the Single Motor judged the best-balanced everyday pick
Spacious, near-limo-like rear seat and a large, usefully square 526-litre boot
Classy, well-finished interior with a crisp 15.4-inch Android Automotive infotainment system
Strong ownership package: 5-year/100,000km free servicing and 5-year unlimited-kilometre warranty
Undercuts key premium EV rivals such as the Porsche Macan Electric on price
cons: No rear window: the camera-fed digital mirror lacks the depth perception of a real mirror, and at least one reviewer reported a passenger became carsick watching the live feed

Near-total reliance on the touchscreen and touch-sensitive steering wheel controls for basic functions like mirrors, seat heating and cruise control fine-adjustment, which reviewers flagged as fiddly and distracting
Lengthy, expensive options list (Plus Pack, Pro Pack, Nappa leather) means the well-equipped price climbs well past the base figure
DC fast-charging speed is competent but trails class-leading rivals
Polestar's smaller Australian dealer and service footprint compared to established luxury brands

summary: The Megane E-Tech is Renault's compact electric hatch, sold in Australia in a single Techno EV60 grade with a 60kWh battery and 454km of WLTP range. Australian reviewers consistently rate it as one of the better-driving and more genuinely efficient EVs in its class -- a long-term test returned 14.4kWh/100km over 2359km -- and repeated price cuts have taken it from a $64,990 launch price to a permanent $54,990 before on-roads. Where opinion divides is on whether the sharp styling and hatch-like driving manners make up for a firm ride on its standard 20-inch wheels, a tight rear seat, and an ownership package (5 years/100,000km, 7.4kW AC charging) that trails most rivals.
pros: Genuinely efficient in the real world: CarsGuide's long-term test averaged 14.4kWh/100km over 2359km and 13.6kWh/100km in city running, beating the 15.6kWh/100km WLTP claim, so the modest 60kWh pack stretches further than the spec sheet suggests

Drives like a hatch rather than a heavy EV crossover -- 4200mm long, 1642kg, quick steering and 0-100km/h in about 7.0 seconds -- and Australian reviewers rate it at or ahead of the Cupra Born and MG 4 for handling

The list price has fallen $10,000 from the $64,990 launch figure to a permanent $54,990 before on-roads, and Renault has repeatedly run drive-away campaigns as low as $45,990-$49,990, so there is unusual room to negotiate

130kW DC charging delivers a 15-80% top-up in roughly 30 minutes, quicker than most 60kWh-class rivals, and it carries a five-star ANCAP rating (2022 Euro NCAP) with AEB, blind-spot monitoring and adaptive cruise standard
cons: Warranty is 5 years/100,000km, not the 5 years/unlimited km nearly every rival offers -- a 20,000km-a-year driver runs out of cover in year five, and Kia's EV3 and MG's 4 both come with seven years
Ride quality on the standard 20-inch wheels and 215/45 tyres is the car's most-criticised trait; reviewers describe bumps and thumps making their presence felt on pock-marked urban roads
AC charging is capped at 7.4kW single-phase, so a full home charge takes over nine hours and a three-phase wallbox buys nothing -- CarsGuide's long-tester called it "a real bummer"

Rear accommodation and the 440-litre boot are tight for family use: toe room is close to non-existent with the front seat low, the centre rear seat is narrow, the boot lip is high and there is no spare wheel

Australian cars go without the connected-services app and some equipment offered in Europe, only the one Techno EV60 grade is sold here, and the updated model (46km more range, higher DC charging power) is not due locally until the first half of 2027

summary: Skoda's compact electric SUV undercuts every other European EV on price in Australia and reviewers consistently rate its efficiency, DC charging speed and conventional, button-rich cabin as class-leading. The split verdict is on ride and range: Australian testers find the fixed-rate suspension too firm for patchy suburban tarmac, and the entry 60 Select's sub-400km WLTP claim asks buyers to pay $7,000 more for the 85 Select to get genuine touring range. Cheap prepaid servicing and a seven-year warranty offset an equipment list that still omits surround-view cameras, sat-nav and a connected app.
pros: 60 Select lists at $48,990 before on-roads, making it the cheapest European-built EV on sale in Australia and priced against Chinese rivals like the BYD Atto 3 and Geely EX5
Genuinely efficient: CarsGuide's long-term 60 Select averaged 15.9kWh/100km, exactly matching the WLTP claim, and CarExpert saw 12.8kWh/100km in the 85
Fast DC charging for the money - the 60 Select peaks at 165kW for 10-80 per cent in about 24 minutes, the 85 at 175kW in about 28 minutes
Prepaid servicing works out to roughly $195 a year over 10 years, with a 7-year/unlimited-km warranty
Rear-drive chassis, 9.3m turning circle and retained physical climate controls; 470L boot expanding to 1580L with Skoda's usual clever storage
cons: Suspension is tuned too firmly for Australian roads - reviewers report a busy, thumping ride over road joins, and no adaptive dampers are offered on Select grades
60 Select's 395km WLTP range is sub-400km; a real-world long-term test returned only 371km, so the 85 Select's 529km costs an extra $7,000
No ANCAP rating as at July 2026 - it relies on a 2025 five-star Euro NCAP result, which can be a blocker for fleet and novated-lease policies
Select grades go without surround-view camera, satellite navigation, vehicle-to-load and a spare tyre, and lack the connected app, remote climate and over-the-air updates rivals include
Lane-keeping assistance is over-sensitive and needs resetting each drive, a common complaint across Australian first drives

summary: The Enyaq is Skoda's mid-size electric SUV and the larger sibling to the Elroq, sold in Australia as a conventional SUV and a fastback Coupe across 60 Select, 85 Sportline and dual-motor RS grades. Australian reviewers rate it highly for packaging, real-world efficiency and a cabin that keeps physical controls, with scores clustered around 8.3/10, but they consistently criticise a firm ride and coarse-chip road noise unless the optional adaptive dampers are fitted. The critical buying decision is the price ladder: everything up to the Coupe 85 Sportline sits under the $75,000 FBT cap for novated leasing, while both RS grades sit just above it.
pros: 85 Sportline lists at $60,990 for 547km WLTP and 210kW, undercutting a Tesla Model Y Premium Long Range AWD ($68,900) and a Kia EV5 GT-Line AWD ($71,770) on range per dollar
Genuinely efficient in Australian conditions: CarsGuide averaged 16.6kWh/100km over 970km in the 85 Sportline and saw 13kWh/100km in city running, against a 15.9kWh/100km WLTP claim
585L boot expanding to 1710L in the SUV with Skoda's Simply Clever storage, plus rear-seat head and knee room reviewers single out as class-leading against the Kia EV5 and BYD Sealion 7
Long, cheap ownership terms: 7-year/unlimited-km warranty (8-year/160,000km battery) with 2-year/30,000km service intervals and a prepaid 8-year/120,000km pack for $1,650, about $206 a year
The RS adds 250kW/545Nm, 5.4s to 100km/h and a bigger 84kWh (79kWh usable) pack charging at up to 185kW DC, so 10-80 per cent takes about 26 minutes
cons: Both RS grades ($76,590 SUV, $77,590 Coupe) sit above the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so a novated lease loses the exemption that the $66,990 Coupe 85 Sportline still qualifies for

Ride is tuned too firmly without the cost-optional adaptive dampers - carsales calls it 'a little too tied down' on bumpy roads and CarsGuide reports intrusive road noise on coarse-chip surfaces with the 21-inch wheels
Only 1000kg braked towing on the 60 Select and 85 Sportline (1200kg on RS), well short of a Tesla Model Y's 1588kg or a Zeekr 7X's 2000kg
No spare tyre at any grade, only a repair kit, and the surround-view camera plus semi-autonomous park assist are options rather than standard on Sportline

Safety rating leans on a 2021 five-star Euro NCAP result for the pre-facelift car with no fresh ANCAP assessment, and the MY27 60 Select's switch to a smaller 61kWh LFP pack has no republished Australian WLTP range yet

summary: The facelifted 2026 Solterra addresses the original car's biggest weaknesses, gaining a larger 74.7kWh battery, more power (252kW combined) and up to 566km of WLTP range, backed by two rounds of price cuts in six months that make it far more competitive. Australian reviewers rate the driving experience highly - composed, quick and comfortable - and praise the upgraded, more premium-feeling cabin, though they still mark it down for tight practicality, some cabin ergonomic quirks and a ride that could use further tuning. Several reviewers suggest the entry AWD variant is the sweet spot of the range, rather than the higher-priced Touring.
pros: Major step up over the outgoing model: bigger battery, +92kW more power and notably longer range
Composed, quick and engaging to drive - CarsGuide rated the driving experience 9/10
Upgraded, more premium-feeling interior with a redesigned console and larger touchscreen
Two price cuts within six months have made it meaningfully more competitive against rivals like the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7
Standard AWD on both variants with a useful 1,500kg tow rating, unusual for a mid-size EV SUV at this price
cons: Practicality trails rivals - CarsGuide scored it just 5/10 on practicality, citing tight boot space and no passenger-side glovebox
Ride quality still needs further tuning - reviewers describe it as firm with more bounciness than ideal
Cabin ergonomic quirks, including an instrument display that can be partly obstructed and an intrusive driver-monitoring system
Repeated price cuts so soon after launch raise doubts about resale value and initial pricing
Touring grade seen as poor value next to the base AWD, which reviewers say is the better buy in the range

summary: Australian reviewers regard the updated Model 3 as the class benchmark among electric sedans, praising a noticeably quieter cabin and softer ride than earlier versions alongside brisk performance and strong efficiency. The Long Range RWD's 750km WLTP claim makes it the longest-range EV sold in the country, while the screen-only control layout continues to split opinion. The Performance variant's near-$81,000 list price also pushes it close to the FBT exemption threshold that keeps novated-lease buyers interested in the cheaper variants.
pros: Long Range RWD offers the longest WLTP range of any EV on sale in Australia at 750km
Access to Tesla's extensive Australian Supercharger network plus regular over-the-air software updates
Recent refresh brings a quieter cabin and noticeably improved ride comfort over the outgoing model
Strong outright performance, with the dual-motor Performance variant hitting 100km/h in around 3.1 seconds
cons: Touchscreen-only interface, including indicators and gear selection on some builds, remains a sticking point for reviewers
Comprehensive insurance premiums tend to sit at the higher end of the EV market due to repair and parts costs
Performance variant's list price sits close to the $75,000 FBT exemption threshold, eroding some of the novated-lease tax advantage

summary: The Model Y is Australia's highest-volume EV, and since the 2025 'Juniper' overhaul Australian reviewers broadly agree it fixed the old car's crashy ride without surrendering its efficiency or Supercharger advantage. The range now runs from the $58,900 Premium RWD to the $89,400 Performance, plus a $74,900 six-seat Model Y L that lands just $100 under the $75,000 mark a novated-lease buyer cares about. Where reviewers split is the cabin: some rate the 16-inch-screen minimalism as fast and uncluttered, others call the car soulless and will not forgive the absence of Apple CarPlay at any price.
pros: Range per dollar leads the segment: $68,900 buys 600km WLTP in the Premium Long Range AWD, and even the $58,900 Premium RWD claims 466km
The Juniper update's adaptive dampers and extra sound deadening are the specific thing CarExpert and Chasing Cars single out as fixing the pre-2025 car's harsh ride and road noise
Model Y L adds a genuinely adult-usable third row and 3.3kW vehicle-to-load for $74,900 — around $20,000 under a Kia EV9 and still inside the FBT-exempt window
Every variant is rated to tow 1,588kg braked, including the entry RWD, and all carry the 5-star 2025 ANCAP result
Tesla lifted its Australian warranty to 5 years/unlimited km for cars delivered from 1 January 2026 (previously 4 years/80,000km), with 5 years of roadside assistance
cons: No Apple CarPlay or Android Auto on any variant — the single most repeated criticism in Australian reviews and a deal-breaker for some buyers
Wipers, mirrors, glovebox and drive modes all live in the 16-inch touchscreen; the Juniper update brought the indicator stalk back but nothing else
The $89,400 Performance costs $20,500 more than the Long Range for 20km less WLTP range, and it is the only variant that pushes a lease past the $75,000 mark
Resale carries Tesla-specific risk: the entry car's list price fell roughly $16,000 across 2023-24, and Tesla now sells a guaranteed-future-value product locally to reassure buyers about it

summary: The updated bZ4X is a much stronger car than the one Toyota launched: a 74.7kWh battery lifts the front-drive model to 591km WLTP and Toyota cut $10,010 off its price, so at $55,990 before on-roads it now undercuts a Tesla Model Y RWD while claiming 125km more range. Australian reviewers agree it is efficient, quiet and far better value than before - scores land between 6.5 and 8 out of 10 - but they split on the chassis, with CarsGuide and carsales calling the ride comfortable and nicely balanced while CarExpert and Chasing Cars find it lumpy above 40km/h with numb steering. The recurring complaints are ergonomic rather than mechanical, and the entry 2WD on 18-inch wheels is the grade most reviewers single out as the pick of the range.
pros: At $55,990 before on-roads the 2WD undercuts a Tesla Model Y RWD ($58,900) and a Kia EV5 Air Standard Range ($56,770) while claiming 591km WLTP against their 466km and 400km
Genuinely efficient rather than just optimistic on paper: 138Wh/km WLTP, and Australian testers recorded 14.4-14.9kWh/100km in mixed driving, so 500km between charges is realistic
AC charging doubled to 22kW three-phase, filling the 74.7kWh pack in about 3h30m - unusually quick for AC and useful if you have three-phase at home
Battery cover extends to 10 years with on-time servicing and the electric motors are warranted for 7, beyond the 8-year/160,000km battery-only cover most rivals stop at
AWD and Touring are rated at 1,500kg braked towing, and the Touring adds a 603L boot and 211mm of running ground clearance without the usual EV load-lip
cons: Its mechanical twin undercuts it: the Subaru Solterra AWD lists at $61,990 against the bZ4X AWD's $67,990, and Subaru bundles five years of scheduled servicing where Toyota charges roughly $180-$190 per 12-month/15,000km visit - the Toyota's counterarguments are the cheaper FWD grade, the longer motor and battery warranty, and a dealer network roughly twice the size
452 litres seats-up is small for a mid-size SUV (a Kia EV5 has 513L, a Model Y 854L) and there is no frunk and no conventional glovebox, so cabin storage is genuinely short

The 7-inch instrument display sits far forward and is partly obscured by the steering wheel rim for taller drivers - flagged by CarExpert, carsales, Chasing Cars and CarsGuide alike, and not fixed by this update
DC fast charging is still capped at 150kW, with Toyota quoting 10-80% in about 45 minutes for the 2WD, so road-trip stops are longer than in an 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 or Kia EV6

Cuts of $10,010 (2WD) and $6,910 (AWD) inside a single model year gutted residuals on earlier bZ4X stock, and no Australian reviewer lists resale as a strength; there is also no spare wheel on any grade, only a repair kit

summary: Toyota's first plug-in hybrid for Australia, launched on the country's best-selling SUV nameplate in late June 2026: a 22.7kWh pack, 113-121km of WLTP electric range and 50kW DC charging, in three grades from $58,840 to $66,340. Reviewers agree the powertrain sets the class benchmark for electric range and refinement and that the car is genuinely quick, but they are just as consistent that once the battery is flat it drinks about 6L/100km - no better than the cheaper conventional hybrid. The argument against it is price rather than execution: it undercuts nothing from BYD or Chery, and without home charging the plug-in premium is money wasted.
pros: 121km of WLTP electric range on the XSE 2WD and 113km on the AWD grades, against 84km for a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and 81km for a BYD Sealion 6 - enough to cover a week of average Melbourne commuting between plug-ins.

50kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in about 30 minutes) and 11kW three-phase AC are standard across the PHEV range, where most plug-in rivals in the class top out at 3.7kW or 6.6kW AC and cannot DC charge at all.
227kW combined in AWD form makes this the quickest RAV4 sold in Australia at around 5.7sec to 100km/h; the 2WD still musters 201kW.
The battery costs less boot than in most plug-in rivals - 655L VDA versus 705L for the non-plug-in RAV4, a 50L penalty rather than the 80-100L several competitors give up.

Five years/unlimited km warranty with no servicing strings attached (driveline cover extends to seven years if you service in the Toyota network), and capped-price servicing at about $325 per visit for the first five services.
cons: Once the battery is depleted it is simply a heavy hybrid: RACV measured 6.0L/100km in HEV mode on an undemanding rural route, no better than the cheaper non-plug-in RAV4, and Toyota specifies 95 RON premium.

Toyota's 0.7L/100km ADR combined-cycle figure is a laboratory artefact that assumes you start every trip fully charged - CarsGuide calls it 'fanciful' - so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home overnight.
Plug-in hybrids lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease maths is far weaker than for a battery-electric rival at the same money, including Toyota's own bZ4X.

At $58,840-$66,340 the PHEV asks roughly $5,000 more than the equivalent hybrid RAV4 and thousands more again than a BYD Sealion 6 or Chery Tiggo 8 PHEV; multiple Australian reviews call the pricing uncompetitive against the Chinese plug-ins.

There is no driver-selectable mode that meaningfully recharges the drive battery on the move, the AWD PHEV carries about 285kg more than the hybrid, and the new-generation RAV4 has no ANCAP rating at launch.

summary: The EX30 is Volvo's compact electric SUV, praised by Australian reviewers for punchy, agile handling, a well-damped ride and a distinctive, upmarket cabin featuring wool-blend seat trim. Sharp price cuts through 2026 have pushed the single-motor Plus below $50,000 before on-roads, making it one of the more attainable premium-badged EVs on the market, and it carries a five-star ANCAP safety rating. It is let down for family duty by a tight rear seat and modest boot, and reviewers are split on whether that's a fair trade-off for its style and driving manners.
pros: Agile, well-controlled handling and a comfortable ride, with brisk acceleration even in the base single-motor form
Distinctive Scandinavian interior design with higher-grade materials, including wool-blend seat trim, that feels a step above rivals
Aggressive 2026 price cuts (Plus from $49,990 before on-roads) bring a premium-badged EV within reach of mainstream buyers
Five-star ANCAP safety rating and strong standard safety tech
cons: Almost every function -- climate control, mirror adjustment, even the glovebox -- is buried in the portrait touchscreen with no driver instrument display; some reviewers call this the car's biggest flaw and report the screen lagging or crashing, while others say it becomes tolerable after a week of familiarity, so opinion is genuinely split rather than uniformly negative
Window switches are relocated to the centre console instead of the doors, one of several cost-saving control choices reviewers find awkward
Small rear seat and boot space limit its practicality as a family car
DC fast-charging speeds are competent rather than class-leading

summary: The EX40 is the renamed XC40 Recharge, a petrol-car-derived compact SUV that Australian reviewers consistently describe as sensible rather than exciting: comfortable, easy to live with and generously equipped, but behind purpose-built EVs on efficiency and packaging. April 2026 price cuts of $7,000 across the range dropped it to $69,990 and $74,990 before on-road costs, which reviewers treat as its strongest argument against a BMW iX1 or Mercedes-Benz EQA. Where opinion divides is whether an eight-year-old platform, a lapsed crash rating and the imminent EX60 make this a run-out bargain or a car worth waiting out.
pros: Both grades were cut by $7,000 in April 2026 to $69,990 and $74,990 before on-road costs, undercutting a BMW iX1 xDrive30 by roughly $8,000 and a Mercedes-Benz EQA 250+ by roughly $11,000 for comparable equipment

Volvo includes five years of complimentary scheduled servicing at 2-year/30,000km intervals plus five years roadside assistance, and covers the drive battery for 8 years/160,000km, so the only routine cost for the warranty period is tyres and electricity
Rated to tow 1,500kg braked as a Single Motor and 1,800kg as a Twin Motor, well clear of the 750-1,000kg typical of compact electric SUVs

There is only one equipment level and it is the top one: panoramic roof, 360-degree camera, Harman Kardon audio and Pilot Assist are standard, with paint, wheels and interior trim the only choices on the configurator

Volvo quotes a 28-minute 10-80 per cent DC recharge on a 200kW charger, and Australian testers recorded 17-18kWh/100km on the road after the 2024 motor and battery update cut the AWD car's consumption from nearly 24kWh/100km
cons: The five-star ANCAP rating it inherited from the petrol XC40 was datestamped 2018 and expired in December 2024, so the EX40 is now sold with no current crash rating -- an odd position for a car bought largely on Volvo's safety reputation

410 litres with the seats up trails a Kia EV6 (480L) and is barely half a Tesla Model Y (854L), and because the body was designed around a petrol drivetrain the front boot is only 31 litres and the load lip is high
The sole Ultra grade rides on 20-inch wheels; reviewers found the ride noticeably firmer than on the 19s the earlier single-motor cars wore, thudding over sharp bumps around town
Regeneration is a single on/off one-pedal switch with no selectable levels, where Hyundai and Kia rivals give you steering-wheel paddles

It is a run-out: the EX60 replacement is due in Australia in late 2026 or early 2027, EX40 sales fell about 40 per cent to 743 units in 2025, and two rounds of price cuts inside a year point to soft resale

summary: The XC60 T8 is the plug-in half of Volvo's mid-size luxury SUV range, sold in Australia only in Plus and Ultra Dark trim alongside the non-plug-in B5 mild hybrids. Reviewers are consistent that it is the calmest and best-finished car in its class and that its 79km WLTP electric range is among the longest of the mainstream premium plug-ins, but they split on whether the money makes sense: at $92,990-$101,990 it is priced against a BMW X3 30e xDrive and a Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e while carrying an ageing cabin architecture and an expired ANCAP rating. The economics rest entirely on charging at home, because with the battery flat it drinks like the petrol SUV it becomes.
pros: 79km of WLTP electric range is well ahead of a Mazda CX-60 PHEV's 62km or a Kia Sorento PHEV's 58km, and Chasing Cars measured just over 70km in real driving — enough that a typical Melbourne commute never wakes the engine.
340kW/709Nm and 4.8sec to 100km/h make the T8 quicker than any petrol XC60 and quicker than the BMW X3 30e xDrive it is priced against.
Rated to tow 2250kg braked, which is 250kg more than a Mazda CX-60 PHEV and unusually strong for a plug-in hybrid.
Five-year unconditional unlimited-kilometre warranty, with the drive battery separately covered for 8 years/160,000km.
Reviewers repeatedly single out ride comfort and noise isolation as the car's real advantage over the German plug-ins rather than outright pace.
cons: The 1.6L/100km label figure only holds if you plug in every night; once the battery is depleted the T8 runs at roughly 8.4L/100km, so a buyer without home charging is paying luxury-PHEV money to run a 2.2-tonne petrol SUV.
AC charging only at 6.4kW and no DC fast-charging, so a full recharge is about three hours on a wallbox and around seven from a household socket — you cannot usefully top up on a road trip.
The battery pack costs 15 litres of boot (468L against the petrol XC60's 483L) and raises the centre tunnel enough that Chasing Cars called the middle rear seat close to unusable.

Both grades sit above the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and far above the $75,000 FBT cap, and PHEVs lost the electric-car FBT exemption on 1 April 2025 — the novated-lease case that carried this car in 2024 no longer exists.
CarExpert notes the XC60's ANCAP rating expired in December 2023 and that the platform is showing its age against newer rivals on cabin tech.

summary: The T8 is the only plug-in XC90 — the B5 grades alongside it are 48-volt mild hybrids with no charge port — and it is currently the only seven-seat plug-in hybrid sold in Australia above $100,000, which is most of its case. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the driving: 340kW, air suspension as standard and a ride-handling balance carsales rated among the best it has sampled in an SUV. Where they diverge is on whether a decade-old platform justifies $130,990, and they agree the numbers are dated — about 69km of WLTP electric range when newer plug-ins clear 100km, AC-only charging, and 7.7L/100km once the battery is flat.
pros: The only seven-seat plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia above $100,000: the Audi Q7, BMW X5 xDrive50e and Mercedes-Benz GLE 450e are all five-seat in their PHEV form, and the cheaper seven-seat plug-ins (Kia Sorento PHEV, Mazda CX-80) sit a full class below on price and equipment

Braked towing is 2400kg, unusually high for a monocoque plug-in hybrid — the Kia Sorento PHEV manages 1010kg and the Mazda CX-80 PHEV 2500kg — so the battery does not cost you a caravan the way it does in most PHEV rivals

Height-adjustable four-mode air suspension is standard on both grades, and carsales rated the resulting ride-handling balance as one of the best it has experienced in an SUV, achieved on 22-inch wheels without any Australian-specific retune

Charge it and the petrol engine barely runs: CarsGuide recorded 3.4L/100km across a week of mixed driving with regular home charging, against 8.1L/100km for the mild-hybrid B5 XC90 that costs about $25,000 less

Volvo's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the high-voltage battery carries a separate eight-year/160,000km cover, and capped-price servicing runs $2380 for three years or $3870 for five on 12-month/15,000km intervals
cons: Charging is AC-only through a 3.6kW onboard charger with no DC capability at all — roughly three hours on a two-phase 6.4kW wallbox, and overnight on a household socket — so a buyer without off-street parking cannot realistically keep the battery full and is left running a 2.4-tonne petrol SUV

Once the battery is depleted it drinks like what it is: carsales measured 7.7L/100km over a week-long loan, and Volvo's own European data quotes 7.2-8.0L/100km with the battery empty, against a 1.8L/100km label figure that assumes you start every trip charged

Electric range is the weak spot of the package — about 69km on WLTP, and both CarsGuide and carsales ran out of battery in the low 60s against the 77km NEDC figure Volvo Australia advertises — at a time when several cheaper plug-in hybrids claim more than 100km

The third row is genuinely awkward: there is no boot-side release, so raising the seats means climbing into the load bay or reaching through a rear door to work a heavy lever, and CarsGuide described the process as too much effort to want to repeat regularly
Boot space behind the raised third row is 262 litres, and there is no spare wheel of any kind — only a repair kit — because of the packaging demanded by the battery pack

summary: The XPeng G6 is a mid-size electric SUV coupe pitched squarely at the Tesla Model Y, with reviewers praising its upmarket cabin, strong tech package and genuinely quick charging on the refreshed 800V architecture. Testers rate the ride and refinement highly and note the flagship AWD Performance model undercuts a comparable Model Y on price while offering vastly stronger acceleration. The main knocks are steering that feels heavy and artificial, a chassis that doesn't quite match the Performance variant's straight-line pace, and quirks like the lack of a glovebox and a fiddly steering-column gear selector.
pros: Upmarket interior fit-out and strong tech/safety suite for the price
Fast 800V/451kW DC charging with a 10-80% top-up around 12 minutes
AWD Performance variant offers Tesla Model Y Performance-rivalling pace at a lower price
Spacious rear seating with good headroom for a coupe-SUV shape
cons: Steering feels heavy and artificial, chassis doesn't fully back up the Performance model's speed
No glovebox and limited cabin storage
Counterintuitive steering-column gear selector
Newer brand with a history of distributor changes in Australia, which may concern some buyers on parts/service continuity

summary: The Zeekr 7X is a mid-size electric SUV that Australian reviewers treat as the most complete Tesla Model Y alternative on price, with an 800V platform, a 615km WLTP Long Range grade and a cabin most testers rate above the Volkswagen ID.4 GTX and Kia EV5 GT-Line for the money. Reviewers agree on the packaging, charging speed and equipment, but split hard on which grade to buy: CarExpert and Chasing Cars both criticise the top grades' adaptive air suspension for bouncing at freeway speeds and prefer the steel-sprung Long Range RWD, while Chasing Cars still rated the Performance AWD 8/10. Recurring complaints are unreliable powered doors, almost everything buried in the 16-inch touchscreen, weak air-conditioning on hot days, no spare wheel, and the unknown resale of a brand that has only sold cars here since 2024.
pros: The $63,900 Long Range RWD is the range sweet spot: 95kWh usable for 615km WLTP, more range than a Tesla Model Y Long Range AWD ($68,900) or any Kia EV5 and for less money, with The Beep recording 500-550km at a sustained 110km/h

800V architecture with a 450kW DC peak on the RWD and Long Range and 22kW AC charging across the range - Chasing Cars timed the Performance AWD's 10-80 per cent DC charge at 16 minutes, and 22kW AC is double or triple the 7-11kW most rivals accept

Rated to tow 2000kg braked on every variant, against 1588kg for a Tesla Model Y, 1250kg for a Kia EV5 and 750kg for a BYD Sealion 7 Premium, with a 539L boot, 1978L seats folded and a 62L frunk on a 2900mm wheelbase

Ownership costs are unusually well defined for a new brand: five-year capped-price servicing totals $2,385 ($477 a year) on 12-month/20,000km intervals, with five years unlimited-km warranty, five years roadside assistance and an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty carrying a 70 per cent state-of-health guarantee

Equipment at the price includes a 36-inch head-up display, 16-inch touchscreen, 21-speaker audio, heated, ventilated and massaging front seats and tri-zone climate on the Long Range and above, and the 7X scored five stars under Euro NCAP with 91 per cent adult occupant protection
cons: The $75,900 Black Special Edition adds only cosmetics over the $72,900 Performance AWD - black wheels, black exterior trim and black Nappa leather, with no mechanical change - yet it is the one variant that sits above $75,000, so it loses the full novated-lease FBT exemption that applies to the rest of the range from 1 April 2027; a $3,000 styling pack that can cost several times that in lease terms

Adaptive air suspension on the Performance AWD and Black Special Edition is the biggest single criticism: CarExpert calls it flimsy at freeway speeds, bouncing dramatically over bumps as it auto-lowers, and explicitly recommends the steel-sprung Long Range RWD instead; Chasing Cars separately found front seats short on lateral support

Powered doors are called unreliable by both CarExpert and Chasing Cars - they misbehave on steep driveways and CarExpert raises a finger-pinch concern - and almost every function including climate control sits in the 16-inch touchscreen with very few physical controls

Chasing Cars measured the Performance AWD at 18.1kWh/100km on the highway and 19.7kWh/100km around town against a 17.5kWh/100km WLTP claim, so plan on roughly 480-520km rather than 543km, and both it and CarExpert flag weak, noisy air-conditioning in Australian summer heat plus no spare wheel, only a repair kit

Resale is unquantified: Zeekr has only sold cars in Australia since 2024, and the sibling Zeekr X was repriced down $5,000-$10,000 in a single model year, so there is no evidence 7X list pricing will hold despite the 2,200 sales achieved by March 2026

summary: The Zeekr X is a compact premium-badged electric SUV that Australian reviewers rate highly for cabin materials, standard equipment and outright pace, with the MY26 update adding 50kW per variant and repricing the range to flat drive-away figures of $48,900 (RWD) and $57,900 (Performance AWD). Opinion is genuinely split on the chassis: CarsGuide rates it one of the more engaging small SUVs to drive, while CarExpert and EV Central find the ride firm and the body underdamped over broken Victorian back roads. The consistent criticisms are a menu-heavy touchscreen, hyperactive driver-assistance chimes, a 405-415km WLTP range that trails cheaper rivals on real-world testing, and the ownership unknowns of a brand that only arrived in Australia in 2024.
pros: MY26 repricing to $48,900 drive-away for the RWD lands it under the Volvo EX30 and well under a BMW iX1 while adding 50kW (now 250kW) and cutting the 0-100km/h claim to 5.6 seconds

Cabin is the standout at the price: quilted leather, 13-speaker Yamaha audio and heated front and rear seats are standard, with massaging front seats and a temperature-controlled fridge on the AWD, and reviewers consistently rate the materials above mainstream rivals such as the Geely EX5 and BYD Atto 3
The RWD's 61kWh LFP pack accepts up to 230kW DC charging for a 10-80 per cent top-up in about 18 minutes, comfortably quicker than the Volvo EX30 or Kia EV3 at similar money, plus 11kW AC
365kW Performance AWD claims 0-100km/h in 3.7 seconds, quicker than anything else in the small electric SUV class
Five-star ANCAP rating, a 1600kg braked tow rating and a 404L boot that is 42L larger than the MY25 car
cons: 405-415km WLTP range is short for the money, and Australian testers recorded 16.5-20.7kWh/100km against the 15.5kWh/100km claim (carsales measured 20.7), so plan on roughly 300-350km between charges rather than 400

Driver-assistance calibration is the near-universal complaint across CarExpert, carsales and CarsGuide: overspeed warnings that repeatedly cut the audio, an attention monitor that chimes on ordinary head checks, and lane-centring that tugs at the wheel

Almost every function including drive modes, seat adjustment and climate is buried in a menu-heavy touchscreen, and reviewers report the reversing camera hijacking the display and wireless CarPlay microphone dropouts

Service and support proposition is thin for a five-year commitment: about 16 Zeekr retail and service sites nationally (three in Melbourne plus Geelong, nothing in Tasmania or the NT), MY26 servicing moved to 12-month/20,000km intervals at roughly $614 a visit and $3,072 over five years, and the standard warranty is five years unlimited km now that the seven-year pre-order offer closed on 31 May 2026, where a Volvo EX30 includes five years of free servicing

Resale is an unquantified risk on a brand first sold here in 2024, and Chasing Cars notes MY26 prices dropped $5,000-$10,000 in a single model year, which immediately devalues the outgoing cars and gives no reason to expect the MY26 pricing to hold
